setInfo: CoroCoro Comic #223 glossy promo (unnumbered), Japan
description: The genuine first Pokémon card ever released to the public. On October 15, 1996, the November issue of CoroCoro Comic — a Japanese monthly manga magazine from Shogakukan — hit newsstands with a two-card glossy insert of Pikachu and Jigglypuff. It landed five days before the Pokémon Trading Card Game officially went on sale. The cards were glued onto a sheet bound inside the magazine and had to be physically peeled out, which is why genuinely undamaged copies barely exist.
funFacts: Predates the official Pokémon TCG launch by five days — manga readers had it before the game was on shelves
The card credits Ken Sugimori as illustrator, but the real artist was Keiji Kinebuchi — an error on the very first Pokémon card ever printed
Because the cards were glued into the magazine, decades of damage means not a single PSA 10 is known to exist
estimatedValue: Enormous but volatile — sealed CoroCoro #223 issues have been valued near $150,000, while peeled singles vary wildly with condition

setInfo: Topps TMNT Series 1, 88 cards + 11 stickers
description: The first ever Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles trading card set, released by Topps to ride the wave of the franchise's animated series and first feature film. It kicked off a run of TMNT card sets that continued into the 1990s.
funFacts: Arrived at the peak of "Turtlemania," riding the first animated series and feature film
One of the earliest properties to successfully cross from Saturday-morning cartoon to trading card aisle
Set the template Topps would reuse for countless licensed-cartoon card sets through the '90s
estimatedValue: $5 – $50 for common cards, more for high-grade or rare inserts

setInfo: Bandai 1st Generation, Japan, #9
description: Most fans assume Konami's 1999 Official Card Game (Vol.1) was the first Yu-Gi-Oh! trading card, but Bandai actually released cards a year earlier, starting April 4, 1998, to tie into Toei's original anime. Blue-Eyes White Dragon appeared as card #9 in that very first Bandai generation — making this, not Vol.1, the true first Yu-Gi-Oh! trading card. Konami only took over the license in early 1999 after Bandai's final set.
funFacts: Predates the Yu-Gi-Oh! OCG that most fans think of as "the first" set by almost a year
Used a simpler dice-and-life-points system, not the card-battle rules Konami introduced in 1999
Bandai's cards are notoriously hard to find in top grades, making high-grade copies genuinely rare
estimatedValue: $20 – $300, more for high-grade examples — these thin, glossy cards are notoriously hard to find in top condition

setInfo: Topps Nintendo Game Pack (with an earlier 1982 Topps Donkey Kong "Jumpman" card predating the Mario name)
description: Mario's trading card history is a bit tangled: his earliest card appearance is arguably the 1982 Topps Donkey Kong set, where he appears as "Jumpman" before the Mario name existed. The first card set to use the Mario/Nintendo branding directly was the 1989 Topps Nintendo Game Pack. A proper full "Super Mario Bros." set from Topps in the US never actually happened.
funFacts: His actual first card appearance predates the "Mario" name itself
Nintendo's mascot never got a proper dedicated Super Mario Bros. set from Topps in the US — a genuine gap in the hobby
A great example of how "the first card" can be a legitimately disputed title
estimatedValue: $5 – $40 depending on card and condition

setInfo: Upper Deck Entertainment SpongeBob SquarePants Trading Card Game, Base Set
description: The first SpongeBob SquarePants trading card set, published by Upper Deck Entertainment on May 27, 2003 as a collectible card game tied to the show, four years after it first aired.
funFacts: Arrived four years after the show's debut, once its popularity was undeniable
One of the first major 2000s cartoons to get a full collectible card GAME, not just a sticker set
Rode the early-2000s CCG boom that followed in the wake of Pokémon and Yu-Gi-Oh!
estimatedValue: $5 – $30, more for first-edition or holo variants

setInfo: Gum, Inc. Mickey Mouse Set (R89/R90), 120 cards
description: Long before modern licensed card sets, Philadelphia's Gum, Inc. produced the first widely-distributed Mickey Mouse trading cards in 1935. Card fronts featured colorful comic-style artwork of Mickey and friends, while the backs carried jokes and trivia questions — one of the earliest examples of Disney characters hitting the collectible card market.
funFacts: Among the very first licensed non-sports trading cards of any Disney character, decades before modern sets
The 120-card set paired jokes and trivia on the back — an early example of "edutainment" card design
A cornerstone of the vintage non-sports card hobby; well-preserved examples are genuinely rare
estimatedValue: $20 – $500+ depending on card and grade; rare high-grade examples can go much higher

setInfo: Walt Disney's Winnie the Pooh 'Card Library' — Pooh Rummy / Concentration / Honey Tree (1965)
description: Pooh is one of the hardest 'first cards' to pin down. Despite being the third highest-grossing franchise on earth, he never got a classic gum-card debut. The earliest widely-collected Pooh card product is this 1965 Walt Disney 'Card Library' boxed set — three card games in one 39-cent pack — rather than a true collectible trading set. Dedicated Pooh trading cards only really arrive decades later.
funFacts: One of the biggest franchises in history with no clean 'rookie card' — a genuine gap in the hobby
The 1965 release is a boxed set of card games, not a collectible trading set
A. A. Milne created Pooh in 1926; Disney only licensed him in 1961, which is why no pre-war card exists
estimatedValue: $30 – $200 for a complete boxed 1965 set, depending on condition

setInfo: Topps Star Wars Series 1 (Blue Border), #1 of 66
description: Released in June 1977, weeks after A New Hope hit cinemas, Topps' blue-bordered Series 1 was the first Star Wars trading card set ever made. Card #1 is a profile portrait of Luke Skywalker, and it sits at the head of the checklist as the franchise's undisputed rookie card. Packs held seven cards and one sticker, with card backs carrying story summaries and multi-card puzzles.
funFacts: A PSA-graded Luke Skywalker #1 has sold for $268,400, one of the highest prices ever paid for a non-sports card
Topps rushed the set out mid-release because nobody predicted how big the film would be
The blue border is the tell — Topps ran five colour-coded series for the first film alone
estimatedValue: $20 – $2,400 for a PSA 8; six figures for top-pop examples of card #1

setInfo: Chocolat Menier Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs trade cards (France)
description: Disney Princess is a licensing banner created in 2000, so it has no debut card of its own. The nearest real card belongs to the princess who started it. Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs opened in 1937, and by 1938 the French chocolate maker Menier was giving away numbered Snow White trade cards with its bars — sixty-two years before anyone thought to group the princesses into a brand.
funFacts: Predates the Disney Princess brand by sixty-two years
Given away with chocolate bars rather than sold — the standard way European trade cards reached children
Snow White was Disney's first animated feature and the first Disney Princess, so her cards start the whole line
estimatedValue: $5 – $40 per card; complete numbered runs are much scarcer

setInfo: Banpresto Anpanman Carddass prism cards (Japan)
description: Anpanman does have trading cards — they are simply Japanese and almost invisible to Western collectors. Banpresto produced Anpanman Carddass prism cards from at least 1991, dispensed from the same coin-operated vending machines that sold Dragon Ball Carddass. Sets continued through the 1990s. The franchise earns tens of billions from toys and food licensing, so the cards remain a minor footnote, but they exist.
funFacts: Sold through Carddass vending machines, the same system as Dragon Ball
Almost unknown outside Japan, which is why the franchise is often assumed to have no cards at all
Anpanman out-earns most household names on this list almost entirely through toddler merchandise
estimatedValue: $5 – $60 per prism card; Western supply is thin

setInfo: Mattel Barbie Series 1 / Deluxe First Edition Portfolio (No. 5533), 300 cards
description: Barbie had been on shelves for three decades before she got trading cards. Mattel's 1990 Series 1 set ran to 300 cards documenting Barbie's outfits and eras, and was also sold as a Deluxe First Edition portfolio in a vinyl binder containing all 300 plus 20 cards exclusive to that package.
funFacts: Arrived 31 years after the doll launched in 1959 — an unusually long wait for a first card
The cards function as a fashion archive, cataloguing outfits year by year rather than telling a story
The 20 portfolio-exclusive cards are the chase pieces for set collectors
estimatedValue: $25 – $120 for a complete sealed Deluxe First Edition portfolio

setInfo: Donruss Marvel Super Heroes #12 — Iron Man run, cards 12–22
description: The MCU is a film continuity rather than a character, so it has no debut card of its own. The nearest thing is the card of the hero who started it: Iron Man launched the MCU in 2008, and his own first card is #12 in the 1966 Donruss Marvel Super Heroes set — the same 66-card run that debuted Spider-Man and Captain America, forty-two years earlier.
funFacts: Iron Man launched the MCU in 2008, but his first card predates the film by forty-two years
Shares its set with Spider-Man and Captain America — all three debut in the same 66 cards
Every MCU hero already had decades of card history before the film series existed
estimatedValue: $50 – $1,500 depending on grade; high-grade 1966 Donruss is scarce

setInfo: Wizards of the Coast Harry Potter TCG Base Set, #8/116 (Holo)
description: Wizards of the Coast — the publisher of Magic: The Gathering — launched the Harry Potter Trading Card Game in August 2001, three months ahead of the first film. The 116-card Base Set drew entirely on Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone. It became the second best-selling toy in the United States before Wizards abruptly stopped printing it after the 2003 expansion.
funFacts: Launched before the first film, so the artwork is book-based rather than film-based
Briefly the second best-selling toy in the entire US market
Wizards killed the game in 2003 and never publicly explained why
estimatedValue: $2 – $60 per card; holographic Harry Potter and Quidditch cards command the most

setInfo: Sanrio Hello Kitty playing card deck (Japan, © 1976)
description: Hello Kitty launched in 1974, and Sanrio was printing her onto cards within two years. The 1976 Japanese playing card deck is the earliest Hello Kitty card product collectors track — a playing deck rather than a collectible set, the same pattern as Winnie-the-Pooh's 1965 boxed card games. Prism and sticker cards followed through the 1980s and 90s, but a structured collectible trading card line only arrived with Sanrio Collector's Card Plus in 2023, a 47-year wait.
funFacts: Sanrio was printing Hello Kitty onto cards within two years of creating her
Beware the date: Sanrio prints the copyright year, so a 1976 mark does not always mean a 1976 printing
A proper collectible trading card line took until 2023 — 47 years after the first deck
estimatedValue: $30 – $250 for a sealed vintage deck depending on condition

setInfo: Upper Deck Call of Duty League, first full trading card release
description: Call of Duty has been one of the biggest entertainment franchises since 2003, but it took until 2021 to get real trading cards. Upper Deck's Call of Duty League set — alongside a Mountain Dew Game Fuel promotional release the same year — put professional esports players rather than in-game characters on cardboard, covering the Modern Warfare 2019 and Cold War seasons.
funFacts: The cards feature real esports pros, not the game characters — unusual for a video game franchise
An 18-year wait between the first game and the first official card set
Part of a broader push to make competitive gaming collectable like traditional sport
estimatedValue: $1 – $50 per card; autographed pro cards fetch more

setInfo: Topps Batman "Black Bat" #1
description: Topps rushed out several Batman sets in 1966 to ride the Adam West television series, and the Black Bat #1 is recognised as the first mainstream trading card of the character. The artwork across the 1966 Batman releases was painted by Norman Saunders, the illustrator behind Mars Attacks, giving the cards their lurid pulp-comic look.
funFacts: A Black Bat #1 has sold at auction for $45,000
Painted by Norman Saunders, the same artist behind the notorious Mars Attacks set
Superman got cards in 1940, but Batman waited until the TV show — 26 years with no Batman card at all
estimatedValue: $50 – $45,000 depending on grade; the #1 card carries a huge premium

setInfo: Donruss Marvel Super Heroes #34 (of 66)
description: The 1966 Donruss Marvel Super Heroes set was the first Marvel trading card release of any kind, and card #34 is Spider-Man's debut on cardboard — just four years after he first appeared in Amazing Fantasy #15. The 66-card set is split into six 11-card character runs, with Spider-Man occupying #34 through #44, each showing a bright comic-panel illustration inside a white border.
funFacts: The first Marvel trading card set ever made, so it doubles as the debut card for Captain America, Thor and the rest
PSA receives more submissions from the Spider-Man run than any other section of the set
Arrived only four years after Spider-Man was created, making it an unusually early character debut
estimatedValue: $100 – $3,000+ depending on grade; high-grade #34 examples are scarce

setInfo: Hasbro / Milton Bradley Transformers Action Cards, 192 cards
description: Milton Bradley published the first Transformers trading cards in 1985, a 192-card run covering Autobot and Decepticon profiles plus scenes from the Generation 1 cartoon. They were sold in eight-card hanger packs rather than wax packs, and every pack included one of 24 mini stickers carrying a character's motto.
funFacts: Printed on playing-card stock with rounded corners, so they feel nothing like a normal trading card
Sold in oversized hanger packs designed to hang on retail pegs beside the toys
Series 1 was the only series ever produced in the US — all 192 cards came out at once
estimatedValue: $1 – $30 per card; sealed 1985 packs command a strong premium

setInfo: Bandai Naruto: The Path to Hokage (Japan), card 忍-1 / Ninja-1, 127 cards
description: Like Yu-Gi-Oh!, Naruto's real first card is Japanese and predates the version Western fans know. Bandai launched Naruto: The Path to Hokage in Japan in 2002, a 127-card set built from Ninja, Jutsu and Mission cards. Uzumaki Naruto is card 忍-1 — literally Ninja-1, the first card of the first set. The English-language Naruto CCG only followed in 2006 and ran until 2013.
funFacts: Card 忍-1 means Ninja-1 — it is literally the first card of the first Naruto set
Predates the English-language Naruto CCG that most Western fans think of as the original by four years
The card is printed with BANDAI 2002 MADE IN JAPAN along the bottom edge, dating it beyond doubt
estimatedValue: $1 – $80 per card; early rare foils are the chase pieces

setInfo: No trading card release
description: Dungeon Fighter Online is one of the highest-grossing games ever made, earning tens of billions almost entirely from in-game microtransactions in China and South Korea. It has essentially no Western merchandising footprint, and no physical trading card line has ever been produced for it.
funFacts: Out-earns most household-name franchises while being nearly unknown in the West
Revenue comes from in-game purchases rather than any physical merchandise
A clear example of how modern free-to-play economics can bypass collectibles entirely
estimatedValue: Not applicable — no trading cards exist
noCardReason: Dungeon Fighter Online earns its money through in-game microtransactions in Asian markets and has almost no physical merchandising, so no trading card set was ever made.

setInfo: Topps Chrome Disney #50 (shown: Orange Wave parallel, 21/25)
description: Cars is the franchise with no rookie card. When the film landed in 2006, Disney funnelled the merchandising into die-cast vehicles — one of the best-selling toy lines ever made — and never commissioned a debut trading card set the way Toy Story and The Lion King got from SkyBox. Lightning McQueen only properly reached cardboard with Topps Chrome Disney, roughly two decades late. Card #50 is his, and it runs all the way up to a one-of-one Superfractor.
funFacts: A top-20 global franchise that went nearly twenty years without a proper trading card set
Disney put the collectible money into die-cast vehicles instead — billions of dollars of little metal cars
The Topps Chrome #50 McQueen tops out at a Superfractor numbered 1/1, the only one in existence
estimatedValue: $5 for a base card up to five figures for the 1/1 Superfractor

setInfo: No trading card release
description: Candy Crush Saga has generated around twenty billion dollars, but it is a mobile puzzle game with no characters, no narrative and no collectible culture. King has licensed it into board games and slot machines, never into trading cards.
funFacts: Among the highest-grossing franchises on earth with essentially no characters to put on a card
Its entire revenue comes from in-app purchases rather than merchandise
Shows how the modern mobile era broke the old link between popularity and collectibles
estimatedValue: Not applicable — no trading cards exist
noCardReason: Candy Crush is a mobile puzzle game with no characters or story to build a card set around, so no trading cards were ever released.

setInfo: Upper Deck Comic Ball 1 — the first major Looney Tunes set
description: Looney Tunes cards are genuinely hard to date. Scattered Bugs Bunny cards turn up as far back as the 1960s, but they were regional novelties that the hobby never properly catalogued. The first major, widely-collected Looney Tunes release is Upper Deck's Comic Ball in 1990, which paired the characters with real baseball players — most famously Bugs Bunny alongside Nolan Ryan.
funFacts: Bugs Bunny cards exist from the 1960s, but they are so poorly documented that no one agrees which came first
Comic Ball is a genuine crossover — real MLB players sharing cards with cartoon characters
Upper Deck ran several Comic Ball series through the early 1990s off the back of its success
estimatedValue: $1 – $40 per card; Bugs Bunny and Nolan Ryan cards carry the premium

setInfo: SkyBox Toy Story, 90-card base set
description: SkyBox produced the first Toy Story cards in 1995 for the release of the first fully computer-animated feature film. Just over half the 90-card base set retells the story, with the rest given over to puzzle cards, pop-ups, and a final run of sixteen cards that assemble into models of four lead characters, four cards per character.
funFacts: Documents the first ever fully computer-animated feature film as it happened
Sixteen cards in the set are body parts that build into four character models
Designed for kids to cut up and play with, so undamaged sets are harder to find than they should be
estimatedValue: $15 – $60 for a complete 90-card base set

setInfo: SkyBox The Lion King Series 1, 90 cards
description: SkyBox's 1994 Lion King set was one of the biggest movie card releases of the decade. Series 1 runs to 90 cards retelling the film and covering the main characters, followed by an 80-card Series 2. Beyond card shops, the cards were handed out in Burger King Kids Meals, putting them in front of a huge audience.
funFacts: Distributed through Burger King Kids Meals as well as hobby shops
Series 1 and 2 together run to 170 cards — an unusually deep set for a single film
Lenticular and other interactive inserts made it one of the flashiest movie sets of the 1990s
estimatedValue: $15 – $50 for a complete Series 1 set; inserts are worth more

setInfo: Panini Dora the Explorer album stickers (Nickelodeon licensed)
description: Dora never got a collectible trading card set, but she is not entirely absent from cardboard. Panini ran licensed Dora album sticker collections through the early 2010s, sold in supermarket packs to be stuck into a book. These are stickers rather than numbered trading cards — the nearest equivalent the franchise has, and typical of how pre-school properties are merchandised.
funFacts: Stickers to be glued into an album, not numbered cards to collect and grade
Sold in supermarkets across Europe and Latin America rather than hobby shops
Pre-school franchises rarely get true card sets — the audience is too young to chase a checklist
estimatedValue: Under $1 per sticker; sealed packs and filled albums carry the value

setInfo: Fleer Pac-Man Stickers & Rub-Offs, 54 cards
description: Fleer put Pac-Man on cardboard in 1980, the same year the arcade cabinet arrived, making it one of the earliest video game trading card sets ever produced. The 54-card run pairs stickers with scratch-off rub-off game cards, and packs shipped with three stickers, three rub-offs and a stick of gum. Fleer followed it with Ms. Pac-Man in 1981 and Super Pac-Man in 1982.
funFacts: One of the first trading card sets built around a video game rather than a film or TV show
Packs contained an actual playable element — scratch-off rub-off game cards
Fleer moved fast: cards were on shelves the same year the arcade machine launched
estimatedValue: $2 – $40 per card; sealed wax packs and complete sets fetch more

setInfo: Panini Paw Patrol album stickers — sticker #1 (Spin Master / Nickelodeon)
description: Paw Patrol has no collectible trading card set, but Panini has run licensed album sticker collections since 2015 — Big Truck Pups, Search & Rescue and others, sold in supermarket packs. These are stickers to fill a book rather than numbered cards to chase and grade, which is the standard pattern for pre-school properties.
funFacts: Stickers for an album, not numbered trading cards with a gradeable checklist
Panini has run several Paw Patrol collections since 2015 and still does
Same pattern as Dora: enormous pre-school revenue, almost no collector card culture
estimatedValue: Under $1 per sticker; filled albums are the collectible unit

setInfo: Peanuts trading cards, first collectible series (1991)
description: Peanuts ran in newspapers from 1950 and its characters appeared on all kinds of printed novelties, some carrying 1958 and 1965 copyright dates. But the first proper Peanuts trading cards the hobby tracks arrive in 1991, timed to the strip's 40th anniversary, followed by ProSport's Peanuts Classics series. Four decades is one of the longest waits for a first card of any major franchise.
funFacts: Peanuts waited four decades from its 1950 debut before getting a real trading card set
Earlier Peanuts card novelties exist with 1958 and 1965 copyright dates, but none were collectible sets
Cryptozoic revived Peanuts cards decades later for the strip’s 75th anniversary
estimatedValue: $10 – $40 for a complete 33-card set

setInfo: Donruss Marvel Super Heroes — no dedicated Avengers debut set
description: The Avengers have no debut card of their own. The team formed in 1963, and its members first reached cardboard in the 1966 Donruss Marvel Super Heroes set — the same 66-card run that gave Spider-Man his first card — where Captain America, Thor and the others appear as individual heroes. A trading card set built specifically around the Avengers as a team would not arrive for decades.
funFacts: Shares its debut set with Spider-Man: the same 1966 Donruss release covers both
The Avengers appear as separate heroes, never as a team, on their earliest cards
The MCU made the Avengers a household name 45 years after their first cards
estimatedValue: $50 – $1,500 depending on hero and grade

setInfo: Topps Disney Frozen Trading Card Game, 170 cards — Glitter Card #98 Elsa
description: Frozen became the highest-grossing animated film ever made, and Topps' European arm answered in 2014 with a 170-card Frozen trading card game — proper packs and boxes rather than a sticker album. Elsa carries the set's top power score of 100, and her glitter card is the one everybody wanted. Panini ran a Frozen sticker album the same year, but these are the film's first actual trading cards.
funFacts: Never sold at retail in North America — Topps released it through its European division only
Elsa's glitter card is scored 100, the highest power value printed in the set
Beyond the base cards there were holographic foils, ice-effect, pop-up and even dot-to-dot cards
estimatedValue: $3 – $15 for glitter and foil singles; sealed 2014 boxes go higher

setInfo: Taito Space Invaders menko card (Japan), © Taito Corp. 1985
description: Space Invaders does have cards, and they are Japanese. Taito licensed Space Invaders menko — thick paper cards used in a floor-slapping game — printed with the arcade's UFO and pixel invaders and stamped © TAITO CORP. 1985. A Shinseisha Taito Game History card followed in 1998. No Western set was ever made, which is why the franchise is usually assumed to have none at all.
funFacts: The card is stamped © TAITO CORP. 1985, so it is officially licensed rather than a bootleg
Menko was the dominant Japanese card format from the 1970s to about 1985 — this one lands right at the end
Fleer put Pac-Man on cards in 1980, but no Western publisher ever did the same for Space Invaders
estimatedValue: $15 – $120 for vintage licensed menko depending on condition

setInfo: Upper Deck World of Warcraft TCG: Heroes of Azeroth, 361 cards
description: Upper Deck launched the World of Warcraft Trading Card Game on 25 October 2006 with Heroes of Azeroth, its first set. Its cleverest idea was the loot card: ultra-rare pulls carrying codes that unlocked real in-game items, like a hippogryph pet or a turtle mount, tying the cardboard directly to the world's biggest MMO. The game ran to 21 expansions before ending in 2013.
funFacts: Loot cards redeemed for real in-game mounts and pets, which sent their prices soaring
Ran to 21 booster expansions between 2006 and 2013
The Warcraft games date to 1994, but nobody printed cards until World of Warcraft made it a phenomenon
estimatedValue: $1 – $60 for most cards; unredeemed loot cards go far higher

setInfo: Topps Despicable Me 3 Trading Card Game
description: The Minions became one of the most merchandised characters of the 2010s, but their first proper trading cards did not arrive until Topps produced a Despicable Me 3 Trading Card Game in 2017 — seven years after the first film. A full Minions collectible card game from Card Fun followed years later, in 2024.
funFacts: Seven years passed between the first film and the first Topps trading card set
The Minions out-merchandised the films themselves long before anyone printed a card
A dedicated Minions collectible card game only arrived in 2024, well over a decade in
estimatedValue: $1 – $15 per card; sealed 2017 packs carry a small premium

setInfo: Leaf Star Trek, 72 cards
description: Leaf produced the first Star Trek trading cards in 1967, a 72-card black-and-white set drawn from episode stills and on-set bloopers. It barely reached the public: Leaf only distributed in Ohio and Illinois, and the set was pulled almost immediately over a licensing dispute. That makes it one of the rarest and most sought-after television card sets in the hobby.
funFacts: Recalled shortly after release over a licensing problem, which is why so few survive
Only ever distributed across Ohio and Illinois — it never went national
The text on the backs was largely invented and often has nothing to do with the episode shown
estimatedValue: $50 – $500+ per card; complete 1967 sets are genuinely rare

setInfo: Bandai Dragon Ball Carddass Set 1 (November 1988), 42 cards
description: Bandai launched Dragon Ball Carddass in November 1988, and Set 1 runs to 42 cards — 36 regular plus 6 prism cards. They were never sold in shops as packs: you fed coins into a Carddass vending machine and it dispensed cards one at a time. The format was a Japanese phenomenon and became the template Bandai reused for countless anime properties.
funFacts: Dispensed from coin-operated vending machines rather than sold in packs
Japan-only, which is why Western collectors discovered them decades late
The six prism cards in Set 1 are the original Dragon Ball chase cards
estimatedValue: $10 – $500+ depending on card and condition; early prisms are the prize

setInfo: Bandai Street Fighter II Carddass (Japan), #27 Chun-Li vs Chun-Li prism
description: Street Fighter follows the same pattern as Yu-Gi-Oh! and Naruto: the Japanese cards came first. Bandai was producing Street Fighter II Carddass prism cards in Japan by 1992, dispensed from vending machines with the same hand-drawn anime artwork Capcom used in its Japanese marketing. Topps only brought Street Fighter II to Western card shops the following year, in 1993, with an 88-card photo-based set.
funFacts: Japanese Carddass prisms beat the American Topps set to market by a year
Dispensed from coin-operated vending machines, exactly like Dragon Ball Carddass
The Japanese cards use hand-drawn anime art; the 1993 Topps set used arcade screen grabs
estimatedValue: $10 – $200 for prism cards depending on character and condition

setInfo: Bandai Demon Slayer wafer card #1 (Japan), Tanjiro & Nezuko
description: Demon Slayer exploded into one of the highest-grossing franchises on earth almost overnight, driven by the Mugen Train film. Its cards followed the modern Japanese pattern: wafer cards, bromides and collectible card releases produced in Japan around 2020 as the anime peaked, rather than a single defining debut set.
funFacts: One of the fastest franchises in history to reach the top 40 highest-grossing list
Its cards arrived during the boom rather than ahead of it, unlike Pokémon
Japanese wafer and bromide cards remain the main collectible format for the series
estimatedValue: $2 – $150 per card depending on rarity and character

setInfo: Topps Jurassic Park #16, 88-card base set
description: Topps released the first Jurassic Park cards alongside the film in 1993. The 88-card base set walks through the plot and covers the characters and dinosaurs, with a sticker in every pack — a Topps house style by that point — and four holograms as the chase inserts.
funFacts: The stickers focus almost entirely on the dinosaurs rather than the human cast
Only four holograms exist in the set, and they are relatively easy to pull
Topps later reissued the artwork as a hardback art book, a rare honour for a movie card set
estimatedValue: $20 – $60 for a complete base set with stickers

setInfo: No trading card release
description: Grand Theft Auto has earned around ten billion dollars and is one of the most recognisable entertainment brands in the world, yet it has never had a trading card set. Rockstar keeps merchandising deliberately minimal, and the adult content rating makes the property a poor fit for a category built largely around kids and family audiences.
funFacts: Rockstar has always kept GTA merchandising unusually sparse by choice
Its mature rating makes it a difficult fit for a traditionally family-facing product category
One of the very few top-40 franchises with essentially no licensed collectibles
estimatedValue: Not applicable — no trading cards exist
noCardReason: Rockstar keeps Grand Theft Auto merchandising deliberately minimal, and the series’ adult rating makes it a poor fit for trading cards. No set has ever been produced.

setInfo: San-X Rilakkuma trading cards (Japan) — 20-card set with holo chase
description: Rilakkuma turns out to have proper trading cards after all. San-X and Bandai have produced Japanese Rilakkuma card sets — the packs are marked トレーディングカード, promise a twenty-card checklist and a possible rare holo, and come one card to a pack. There are Rilakkuma wafer cards too. None of it reaches the West in quantity, which is why the character is usually assumed to be stationery-only.
funFacts: The packs advertise a twenty-card set and a rare holo chase — a real checklist, not a novelty
San-X built the brand on stationery and plush, so the cards are a small sideline
Rilakkuma means 'relax bear' and has no story or cast, which makes a card set an odd fit
estimatedValue: $2 – $25 per card; sealed Japanese packs go for more

setInfo: Japanese Monster Strike wafer cards and TCG (mid-2010s onward)
description: Monster Strike does have physical cards, contrary to what its all-digital reputation suggests. After the game launched in 2013 it spread into Japanese wafer cards — foil cards packaged with a biscuit — plus a full trading card game and movie tie-in sets. They circulate almost entirely within Japan, which is why the franchise is often assumed to be digital-only.
funFacts: Wafer cards are sold with a biscuit in the pack, a distinctly Japanese format
The in-game gacha already works like a card collection, so the physical cards are a supplement rather than the main event
Almost all of its ten-billion-dollar revenue is Japanese, and so is its card market
estimatedValue: $1 – $40 per card; sealed Japanese wafer packs carry a premium

setInfo: Philadelphia Gum James Bond #1, 66 cards (PSA labels the set 1966)
description: Philadelphia Gum produced the first widely available James Bond cards in North America in 1965, a 66-card set drawing on Dr. No, From Russia with Love and Goldfinger. The cards are black-and-white movie stills and promotional shots inside a thin white border, capturing Sean Connery's Bond at the height of the first wave of Bondmania.
funFacts: Covers the first three Connery films in a single 66-card run
Black-and-white photography, at a time when colour card printing already existed
Bond began as novels in 1953, but the cards track the films — this set arrived three years after Goldfinger
Card references disagree on the year — most sources say 1965, PSA slabs it as 1966
estimatedValue: $5 – $80 per card; complete graded sets run into the thousands

setInfo: E-Max / Rovio Angry Birds TCG #001 Red
description: Angry Birds was the defining mobile game of the early 2010s and, unusually for a mobile title, it merchandised hard — plush, films, theme parks and cards. Its trading cards arrived in the early 2010s through European publishers, at the point where the game was briefly one of the most recognised brands on earth.
funFacts: One of very few mobile games to get real trading cards, unlike Candy Crush
Rovio pushed merchandising aggressively while the game was at peak popularity
The card sets are mostly European releases rather than US hobby product
estimatedValue: Under $1 per card; complete albums carry the value

setInfo: Banpresto Thomas the Tank Engine prism cards (Japan), © Britt Allcroft 1992
description: The Railway Series began in 1945, making Thomas one of the oldest franchises on this list, and his first cards are not British or American — they are Japanese. Banpresto produced holographic prism cards in Japan carrying a 1992 Britt Allcroft copyright, using photographs of the original model-railway television series. ERTL followed with a Series 1 trading card set in 1998, and a 100-card Gullane and Briarpatch release came in 2002.
funFacts: Nearly fifty years passed between the first Railway Series book and the first Thomas cards
The earliest Thomas cards are Japanese prism cards, not British or American ones
They use photographs of the physical model railway, years before the show went computer-animated
estimatedValue: $5 – $60 per prism card; Japanese sets are scarce in the West

setInfo: Panini Fortnite Series 1 #235 (Crystal Shard parallel)
description: Panini produced the first Fortnite trading cards in 2019, at the peak of the game's cultural dominance. Series 1 covers the outfits and characters players actually recognised from the battle royale, and it worked: unlike most game tie-ins, Fortnite cards found a genuine collector market and high-grade rare outfits climbed quickly.
funFacts: Reached cards just two years after launch — one of the fastest turnarounds on this list
Rare and Legendary outfit cards became genuine chase pieces almost immediately
Proved a free-to-play game could still support a real physical card market
estimatedValue: $1 – $500+ depending on rarity tier and grade

setInfo: Himitsu Sentai Gorenger menko cards (Japan, mid-1970s)
description: Saban's Mighty Morphin Power Rangers reached American cards in 1994 via Collect-A-Card, but the franchise is Japanese and started in April 1975 with Himitsu Sentai Gorenger. Japanese children were buying Gorenger menko — thick paper cards used in a floor-slapping game — during that original run, nearly twenty years before Power Rangers existed in the West. Menko was the dominant Japanese card format from the 1970s until roughly 1985.
funFacts: Menko are playing pieces first and collectibles second — you slam them down to flip your opponent's card
The Japanese cards predate the American Power Rangers cards by around nineteen years
Exact menko sets are notoriously hard to date: most carry no year and no manufacturer mark
estimatedValue: $10 – $150 for vintage 1970s menko depending on condition and character

setInfo: Iron Crown Enterprises Middle-earth CCG: The Wizards (1995)
description: Tolkien published The Hobbit in 1937, and Middle-earth waited nearly sixty years for cards. Iron Crown Enterprises released the Middle-earth Collectible Card Game in late 1995 — the first Middle-earth cards of any kind — using original artwork from longtime Tolkien illustrators including John Howe, Ted Nasmith and Angus McBride. Topps' familiar photo cards only arrived in 2001 with the Peter Jackson films, six years later.
funFacts: Predates the Peter Jackson films entirely — the art is painted, not photographed
Won the Origins Award for Best Card Game of 1995
Iron Crown lost the Tolkien licence in 1999, ending the game two years before the films arrived
estimatedValue: $1 – $200; original ICE artwork cards are the collector draw

setInfo: Topps Marvel Super Heroes Stickers — die-cut sticker, “I'm a Sight for Sore Eyes!”
description: The X-Men were kept off cardboard for a strangely long time. The 1966 Donruss set that gave Spider-Man and Captain America their debuts skipped them entirely, and so did Topps' 1975 Comic Book Heroes stickers. Their first appearance is here: Topps' 1976 Marvel Super Heroes Stickers, a 40-sticker run of die-cut characters with joke speech bubbles. Only two X-Men made the cut — Cyclops and Ice Man — and Cyclops is the one printed with the team's X-belt in plain view.
funFacts: The 1966 Donruss set covered only Cap, Iron Man, Daredevil, Spider-Man, Hulk and Thor — no X-Men at all
Cyclops and Ice Man were the only two X-Men in the 1976 set; Angel, Beast, Marvel Girl and Professor X were all left out
The first cards built entirely around the X-Men came much later — Comic Images in 1991, then the famous Jim Lee Impel set in 1992
estimatedValue: $30 – $350 for graded singles; ungraded stickers stay inexpensive

setInfo: Gum, Inc. Superman (1940) — shown: #47 Horror Beneath the Sea
description: Superman first appeared in Action Comics #1 in 1938, and Gum, Inc. — the same Philadelphia company behind the 1935 Mickey Mouse cards — put him on cardboard just two years later. The 1940 Superman set is one of the earliest superhero card releases in existence, and card #1 is among the most valuable non-sports cards ever printed.
funFacts: A Gum, Inc. Superman #1 has sold at auction for $36,250
Produced by the same company as the 1935 Mickey Mouse set on this list
Predates the first Batman cards by twenty-six years despite the characters debuting a year apart
estimatedValue: $200 – $36,000+ depending on grade; card #1 carries an enormous premium

setInfo: Gum, Inc. Superman #12 'Superman's Arch Enemy'
description: The DCEU is a film continuity launched in 2013, not a character, so it has no debut card. The nearest real card belongs to the hero who started it: Man of Steel opened the DCEU, and Superman's own first cards are the 1940 Gum, Inc. set — seventy-three years earlier. Card #12, 'Superman's Arch Enemy', even anticipates the conflict the film series would build itself around.
funFacts: Man of Steel launched the DCEU in 2013; Superman's first cards predate it by seventy-three years
Same Philadelphia publisher, Gum Inc., that made the 1935 Mickey Mouse cards in this database
The film series was retired and rebooted as the DCU before it ever established a card identity of its own
estimatedValue: $150 – $3,000 depending on grade; 1940 Gum Inc. cards are fragile and scarce

setInfo: Limited Edition Alpha, 295 cards
description: Magic: The Gathering invented the trading card game. Richard Garfield's design launched in August 1993 as Limited Edition Alpha, a 295-card print run that sold out almost immediately — Wizards of the Coast had expected it to last months. Black Lotus is the most famous card in the game and arguably in the entire hobby: it produces three mana for free and was banned from serious play almost immediately.
funFacts: Created the entire trading card game category — every game in this tab descends from it
Alpha cards have visibly rounder corners than every later printing, a production quirk that makes them instantly identifiable
An Alpha Black Lotus graded PSA 10 sold for $540,000, and a signed copy later went for over $3 million
estimatedValue: Alpha commons run into the hundreds; Black Lotus into six and seven figures

setInfo: Bandai OP-01 Romance Dawn — OP01-003 Luffy Leader (alt art)
description: Bandai launched the One Piece Card Game in Japan on 22 July 2022 with OP-01 Romance Dawn, named after the very first chapter of Eiichiro Oda's manga. The 121-card set introduced the Leader mechanic that defines the game, with eight Leaders anchoring deck construction. It reached the US that December and by late 2025 was outselling Yu-Gi-Oh! in monthly sales.
funFacts: Named after the first chapter of the One Piece manga, published back in 1997
Grew fast enough to overtake Yu-Gi-Oh! in monthly sales within three years of launch
Now the third best-selling trading card game in the world behind Magic and Pokémon
estimatedValue: $1 for commons up to several thousand for graded Romance Dawn secret rares

setInfo: Ravensburger The First Chapter, 204 cards — Elsa Enchanted 207/204
description: Ravensburger launched Disney Lorcana on 18 August 2023 with The First Chapter, giving Disney its first proper trading card game after nearly a century of characters. The 204-card set reimagines Disney characters as 'Illumineers' summoning glimmers, and demand was so far beyond forecast that early print runs sold out instantly and reprints had to be scheduled within months.
funFacts: Disney's first real trading card game, arriving 88 years after the 1935 Mickey Mouse gum cards
Launch stock sold out so fast that Ravensburger announced reprints within weeks
Reached the sixth best-selling TCG in the world within two years of existing
estimatedValue: $1 – $600 depending on rarity; enchanted-rare cards drive the market

setInfo: Bandai Digital Monster Card Game (Japan, June 1999) — shown: Digi-Battle Series 1 #BO-01
description: Bandai released the first Digimon cards in June 1999 as the Digital Monster Card Game, with two further boosters following the same year. An English adaptation, Digi-Battle, arrived shortly after and is what most Western collectors from that era remember. The original game ran until 2005; Bandai rebooted the franchise entirely with a new Digimon Card Game in 2020.
funFacts: Launched the same year Digimon hit Western television, riding the Pokémon boom
The 1999 game ran for six years before being retired in 2005
The English Digi-Battle cards are slabbed as 2000, but the card itself is printed © 1999 BANDAI
estimatedValue: $2 – $300 for 1999 originals; sealed first-edition product goes higher

setInfo: Decipher Star Wars Customizable Card Game, Premiere set
description: Star Wars appears twice in this database. Its first trading cards are the 1977 Topps set in the media tab; its first trading card GAME is Decipher's Star Wars Customizable Card Game, whose Premiere set launched in December 1995. It ran until 2001 and was one of the biggest CCGs of the 1990s. Fantasy Flight's Star Wars: Unlimited revived the idea in 2024 and is now a global top-10 seller.
funFacts: Star Wars is the rare franchise with two separate firsts — 1977 for cards, 1995 for a card game
Decipher ran the game for six years before losing the licence in 2001
Star Wars: Unlimited brought the franchise back to the TCG top ten in 2024
estimatedValue: $1 – $200 for Premiere singles; sealed 1995 product is scarce

setInfo: Legend Story Studios Welcome to Rathe (Alpha) — WTR041 Cold Foil
description: Flesh and Blood launched in October 2019 from Legend Story Studios, a small New Zealand publisher, with Welcome to Rathe. It was built deliberately for in-store play rather than online, with no digital client at all — a contrarian bet in 2019. It worked: the game became a genuine competitor to Magic in the hobby channel and remains a top-10 seller.
funFacts: Made by a small New Zealand studio competing directly with Wizards of the Coast and Bandai
Deliberately launched with no digital version, betting entirely on in-store play
Its rarest early cards, the Cold Foil legendaries, trade for five figures
estimatedValue: $1 – $30,000; first-edition Cold Foil legendaries are the trophy cards

setInfo: Bandai Gundam Card Game GD01 Newtype Rising — GD01-001 RX-78-2
description: Bandai launched the Gundam Card Game in July 2025, and it went straight into the global top five best-selling trading card games in its first quarter — an almost unheard-of debut. Gundam had carried decades of Japanese card products before this, but GD01 is the first unified global trading card game for the franchise.
funFacts: Broke into the worldwide top five best-selling TCGs within a single quarter of launching
Gundam is nearly fifty years old, but this is its first unified global card game
Bandai now runs three of the top ten TCGs: One Piece, Digimon and Gundam
estimatedValue: $1 – $500 depending on rarity; the market is still young and volatile

setInfo: Riot Games / UVS Games — Riftbound: Origins, OGN 034/298
description: Riot Games brought League of Legends to physical cardboard with Riftbound, whose first set Origins launched globally on 31 October 2025. Riot had tried digital cards before with Legends of Runeterra, but Riftbound is the first physical League of Legends trading card game, and it posted one of the strongest debut quarters the category has seen.
funFacts: Riot's first physical card game after years of the digital-only Legends of Runeterra
Launched in China months ahead of the global release, an unusual order of operations
Posted one of the biggest debut quarters of any new TCG on record
estimatedValue: $1 – $400; chase champion cards drive the early market

franchise: The Lord of the Rings TCG
setInfo: Decipher The Fellowship of the Ring, 365 cards
description: Decipher launched The Lord of the Rings TCG in November 2001 alongside the first film, with a 365-card Fellowship of the Ring set. It was not the first Middle-earth card game — Iron Crown's MECCG beat it by six years and appears in the media tab — but it was the first built on the film licence, and it became far the bigger seller of the two.
funFacts: Not the first Middle-earth card game — Iron Crown's 1995 MECCG came first
Decipher had already done the same trick with Star Wars in 1995
Won the Origins Award for best trading card game of its year
estimatedValue: $1 – $150; foil Aragorn and Gandalf cards lead the market

setInfo: Wizards of the Coast / Takara DM-01 Base Set (Japan)
description: Duel Masters is the game Wizards of the Coast built specifically for Japan. Launched in May 2002 with Takara, DM-01 simplified Magic's design into something faster and tied it to a manga and anime. It became one of the biggest card games in Japan — outselling Magic there for years — while barely registering in the West.
funFacts: Designed by Magic's own publisher as a deliberately simpler game for the Japanese market
Outsold Magic: The Gathering in Japan for much of the 2000s
The English release was discontinued in 2006 while the Japanese game kept going
estimatedValue: $1 – $400; early Japanese DM-01 rares carry the value

setInfo: Bushiroad Weiss Schwarz, first trial decks (Little Busters! / D.C. II)
description: Bushiroad launched Weiss Schwarz in Japan in 2007 as a crossover engine: any anime, manga or game licence can be printed into the same rules. The first decks covered Little Busters! and Da Capo II. Nearly two decades on it has absorbed hundreds of franchises, from Attack on Titan to Hatsune Miku to Disney.
funFacts: Built from the start as a crossover system rather than around a single franchise
Has now printed cards for several hundred different anime and game licences
The name means "White Black" in German — the two halves of its colour system
estimatedValue: $1 – $500; signed and SP-rarity character cards go far higher

setInfo: Bushiroad Booster Set 1: Descent of the King of Knights — BT01/S04 SP
description: Bushiroad followed Weiss Schwarz with an original property of its own. Cardfight!! Vanguard launched on 12 March 2011 with Booster Set 1, Descent of the King of Knights, alongside a manga and anime built to promote it. Blaster Blade is the game's signature unit and the face of its first set.
funFacts: Launched simultaneously with its own manga and anime, all designed together as one product
Notably had no cost or mana system, an unusual design choice for a major TCG
Spent years as a top-ten seller before slipping out of the leading pack in 2025
estimatedValue: $1 – $300; early Japanese SP-rarity cards command the most

setInfo: Bandai Union Arena (24 March 2023) — Hunter x Hunter promo
description: Bandai launched Union Arena on 24 March 2023 as a crossover card game spanning its licence portfolio — Hunter x Hunter, Jujutsu Kaisen, Bleach, Code Geass and more sharing one rule set. It followed the Weiss Schwarz model of a franchise-agnostic system, and Bandai brought an English edition to the West at the end of the year.
funFacts: Bandai's answer to Weiss Schwarz, built to monetise its entire anime licence catalogue at once
Launched in Japan first, with the English edition announced only in December 2023
Sells strongly through Japanese channels even where it under-registers on Western marketplaces
estimatedValue: $1 – $250 depending on series and rarity

setInfo: Fantasy Flight Games Spark of Rebellion (8 March 2024)
description: Star Wars returned to the trading card game shelf in March 2024, twenty-three years after Decipher's version ended. Fantasy Flight's Spark of Rebellion introduced a leader-and-base structure and landed straight in the global top ten best-selling card games, where it has stayed.
funFacts: The third distinct Star Wars entry in this database — 1977 Topps cards, the 1995 CCG, and now this
Reached the worldwide top ten within its first year on sale
Its Hyperspace and Showcase parallel treatments drive most of the secondary market
estimatedValue: $1 – $700; Showcase leaders are the chase cards

setInfo: Curiosa — Alpha set (2023), Foil Unique
description: Sorcery: Contested Realm is the most deliberately old-fashioned game in this tab. Designed by Erik Olofsson and published by Curiosa, its Alpha set arrived in 2023 with hand-painted artwork and a board-based playing field, aimed squarely at players who miss what early Magic felt like. A tiny Alpha print run made it an immediate speculation target.
funFacts: Deliberately styled after early-1990s Magic, down to the painted artwork
Played across a spatial board rather than an abstract battlefield, unusual for a TCG
A tiny Alpha print run meant singles were trading for hundreds within weeks of release
estimatedValue: $5 – $2,000; Alpha foils reach four figures
